title: SYSK Selects: How Rabies Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode on rabies (originally released February 9, 2016). Hosts cover the history of rabies, from ancient Mesopotamian laws and the St. Hubert pilgrimages to Louis Pasteur's vaccine. They explain the virus, which attacks the central nervous system and replicates in neurons, spreads mainly through saliva, and has furious and paralytic forms. Other topics include transmission routes (bites, corneal transplants, bats, rare aerosol cases), animal reservoirs (raccoons, bats, dogs), symptoms in animals and humans, hydrophobia, dog vaccination and eradication efforts (including Bali and oral baits in the US), global deaths, post-exposure treatment, the Milwaukee protocol (Gina Geiger's survival), the Peruvian immunity study, the historical belly-injection treatment, and Ozzy Osborne's bat incident. The episode ends with a listener mail about a man's eyeball being forced out of his head in a water-skiing accident.

segments.title: Rerun intro and Old Yeller banter
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the Saturday select of the February 2016 rabies episode. The hosts joke about Old Yeller, which involves a rabid dog being shot, and note that rabies is a virus found on every continent except Antarctica.

segments.title: History and etymology of rabies
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the age of rabies, with early references in Mesopotamian law, the word's roots in Latin and Sanskrit meaning rage or violence, and pilgrimages to St. Hubert in Liege for protection.

segments.title: Pasteur's rabies vaccine
segments.summary: Louis Pasteur developed a rabies vaccine in 1885 using a weakened form of the virus, with the idea that gradual exposure would build immunity. The hosts describe his first human trial on a boy bitten by a dog.

segments.title: How the rabies virus attacks the body
segments.summary: The rabies virus is a bullet-shaped virus that travels through nerves to the spinal cord and brain, where it replicates in neurons. It then moves to the salivary glands, which is the main route of transmission. The hosts describe the furious and paralytic forms.

segments.title: Animal hosts, bites, and rare transmission routes
segments.summary: Rabies is found only in mammals. Raccoons, bats, and other mammals can carry it, and a New Jersey raccoon attack is mentioned. The hosts explain why smaller animals rarely carry it and discuss how it spreads through saliva, rarely through aerosols in a Texas cave, and possibly through kissing, sexual contact, or corneal transplants.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: A short break in the episode before the discussion continues.

segments.title: Rabies testing, symptoms, and bats
segments.summary: The hosts describe how rabies is tested in animals by examining the brain, and list animal warning signs such as nocturnal animals active by day, drooling, and lack of fear of humans. They explain why bats are the main source of human cases in the US, due to their tiny teeth that can bite unnoticed. Chuck suggests a bat episode.

segments.title: Bali, US wildlife vaccine baits, and dog vaccination
segments.summary: Bali was rabies-free until 2008, when dogs spread the virus and people died. The US uses oral vaccine baits in wildlife and has largely eliminated dog-transmitted rabies through pet vaccination laws. The hosts give statistics on US and worldwide deaths, with tens of thousands dying each year, mostly in developing countries.

segments.title: Human symptoms, hydrophobia, and survival cases
segments.summary: The hosts list human symptoms, including anxiety, fever, hallucinations, and sporadic pulse, and explain hydrophobia as a fear of water caused by painful throat spasms. They describe Gina Geiger's survival after a medically induced coma, now known as the Milwaukee protocol, and a Peruvian study of people with apparent immunity.

segments.title: Historical treatment, Ozzy Osborne, and prevention
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1950s to 1980s belly-injection treatment with 20 to 23 shots. They mention Ozzy Osborne biting the head off a bat and receiving rabies shots as a precaution. They discuss pre-exposure vaccination and the advice to see a doctor after an animal bite, then point listeners to the How Stuff Works article.

segments.title: Listener mail: cringe-worthy eyeball story
segments.summary: A listener writes that her father's eyeball was forced out of his socket during a water-skiing accident in Las Vegas, and that he pushed it back in himself and never saw a doctor. The hosts react to the story and close with credits.

segments.title: Outro and credits
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners, ask for submissions, and give credits for the show.
